newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU ends tradition of Europe's note-issuing banks.
newsitem.headline: EMU ends tradition of Europe's note-issuing banks.

text.p: They have survived wars, crises in government and finance and thwarted counterfeiters, in some cases for centuries.
But the handful of private European banks which can print their own notes are now facing their greatest ever challenge: economic and monetary union (EMU).

If some European central bankers get their way, notes issued by the likes of Banque Internationale a Luxembourg (BIL) and the Royal Bank of Scotland will disappear once the Euro replaces national currencies in 2002.
The European Monetary Institute (EMI), which on Friday will present the first common Euro note designs, said the question of private issuers will probably not be addressed until next year.
But one central banker told Reuters that note issues will be subject to the authorisation of the future European Central Bank and it was likely "this historical feature will disappear."
Most of the banks vow to defend their often hard-won right to print and sell their own notes. But they acknowledge that at the moment the future looks uncertain.
"We are hoping to continue but at the moment there are many open questions about EMU and it's too early to say what will happen," BIL spokeswoman Christiane Schmit told Reuters.

"If people decide there has to be a pan-European design that's a political decision. You can have diversity of design. We have 300 years of history to show that is possible," said Alwyn James of the Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS).
BIL and RBS are just two of a handful of issuing banks.

The others are: Scottish banks Bank of Scotland and Clydesdale Bank and Northern Ireland's Ulster Bank (a unit of National Westminster Bank PLC ), Northern Bank, First Trust Bank (a unit of Allied Irish Bank, and Bank of Ireland (a unit of the Irish bank of the same name.
The Scottish and Northern Irish banks retained the right to issue notes after the Bank of England clamped down on private banks issuing notes in England and Wales in 1844.
BIL has held its franchise since 1846.
But in practice their independence is symbolic.
The British banks must back the bulk of the notes they issue with deposits at the Bank of England.

The unbacked currency they issue cannot exceed the total they issued in 1846, RBS's James said. In Royal Bank of Scotland's case, this means around one million pounds out of a total 750 million of RBS notes in circulation.

The banks and the Bank of England also agree on the size and general colour of the notes. James pointed out, however, that this leaves the banks free to determine the design and face value of the notes: in Scotland there are one pound and 100 pound notes, which do not exist in England.
"You could argue this could be done at European level quite easily," James said.
The European Monetary Institute has proposed limiting Europe's future bank notes to 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500 Euros.

BIL has had limits placed on its issuance since 1914. It can now circulate a maximum 50 million Luxembourg francs of its distinctive 100 franc notes compared with the five billion francs of notes circulated by the Grand Duchy's fledgling central bank, the Institut Monetaire Luxembourgeois.
BIL likes to point out that it outlasted the Grand Duchy's last central bank, the Banque Nationale du Grand Duche de Luxembourg, which issued notes from 1873 until its collapse some years later.

In any case, the BIL notes look likely to become collectors' items. The last series was printed in 1981 and the stock is sufficiently large to last until the Euro is introduced after 1999. "We are not planning at the moment to print any more," Schmit said.
The British banks' bid to continue to issue notes is also complicated by the United Kingdom's opt-out on stage three of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
A Bank of England spokesman declined to speculate how the problem might be addressed.

"As far as bank notes are concerned, EMU will not affect us if we are out. The question only arises if we are in and it's at that point this would have to be looked at. Whether we are in or out is a political decision and not for us to comment on," BoE spokesman Vernon Everitt said.
